items.speaker: CHRIS PENK
items.text: Thank you very much, Mr
Speaker—I just got tied up in another matter.
So speaking to the Counter -Terrorism Acts (Designations and Control Orders)
Amendment Bill, I think that the points that the Minister has made, first of all—and then
others, speaking to it—have been well made. I think at this, the second reading, it’s worth
reflecting a little bit on the treatment of the subject at the Justice Committee.
I note the chair of the Justice Committee, Vanushi Walters, has now resumed her seat,
although this was a matter that was discussed at earlier stages within this Parliament. So
while she and other members —including, I see, Dr Emily Henderson, among others —
considered the bill, I think, for the part that I was able to observe from the outside, so to
speak, it seemed to be a good process. It  seemed to be one of careful and good -faith
consideration of some pretty important issues.
I’d like to step through a couple of those issues, but I’d be remiss if I didn’t begin with
an acknowledgment of the fact that in this country, as my colleague and f riend Mark
Mitchell has said, we are not immune to terrorist attacks. While they are mercifully rare,
they are, on the other hand, extremely serious in nature when they occur—most obviously
and most tragically, in terms of number of lives lost, of course, we think of the March 15
atrocity at the mosques in Christchurch and we think particularly of those who lost their
lives that day, those who live still with the memory of that tragedy, and also those who
quickly leapt into action to try to physically defeat the actions of the terrorist and who, no
doubt, live still with the memory of that day.
I emphasise this not to take us far away from the content of the bill, but it’s important
context. The reason that it’s important is because Parliament must, as a res ponsible
lawmaking body—if that’s what we are, at least some of the time —consider situations
that are extreme, that are unusual, as I said before, mercifully so, but in respect of which
there is a risk that is not trivial. And so while we are weighing the restriction on rights
that we impose as a State on individuals whom we incarcerate and otherwise deal with in
a criminal justice manner, we must be mindful of the huge stakes that are involved.
This is, of course, not to say that we should be blasé about the human rights involved,
but it does go to a weighing exercise. Of course, whenever you’re talking about human
rights—and we are talking about human rights, human rights of different parties —it’s
important to weigh, in the balance, those competing rights and considerations. And also
because the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act specifically invites us—indeed, requires us—
to make that consideration when it talks about “justified limitations” on the rights
contained in that Act.
So in this bill, we see that it’ s possible to amend, or that the bill will, in fact, amend
the regime that currently exists in relation to designations and control orders for those
who have been deemed “terrorist”. And that’s not a sort of mere use of vernacular to
indicate disapprobation; in fact, it’s a technical term. It’s a particular definition or, indeed,
designation that is made. So what we’re really grappling with now as a Parliament is the
extent to which we can say that a person who already has that designation attached to
them can be required to remain in that state for the benefit of the community whose safety
will be improved while that person remains in that state and with all the monitoring and
restrictions that go along with it.
Of course, the flip side is that a person who has their liberty deprived—albeit for very,
very, very good reasons—nevertheless might say, if they were here, that their rights are
being breached. One doesn’t have to be too much of a bleeding-heart liberal to say, “Well,
actually, even app roaching the matter from, say, a libertarian perspective, the State
shouldn’t exercise its considerable power against individuals in a reckless or irresponsible
way.” So we say, well, is it reasonable to do as this legislation is doing: restricting a
15800 Counter-Terrorism Acts (Designations etc.) Amdt Bill 30 Mar 2023
person’s liberty to the extent that we are saying that the designation that they have as a
terrorist will continue for longer as a result of this bill?
There’s a retrospective element to some extent, and, as a starting point, no Parliament
should actually want  to be engaged in retrospective lawmaking, except that sometimes
it’s justified. I think it’s important that we do justify it, if we’re engaging in changing of
the law in a way that, effectively, looks backwards. We had, as recently as last night,
some ret rospective or retroactive lawmaking —I can never remember the difference
between those, got a number of—

items.speaker: Marja Lubeck
items.text: Retrospective, I think.

items.speaker: CHRIS PENK
items.text: “Retrospective”, I hear from Marja Lubeck. Do I have any further
bids? I’m looking at Duncan Webb, I’m looking to my right, I think I see a wave of the
hand. If this were an auction, Arena Williams, you would have just bought a house! But
I think you’re probably not engaging in my little game—

items.speaker: Arena Williams
items.text: Wrap it.

items.speaker: CHRIS PENK
items.text: Pardon me. We should wrap it. Well, I don’t want to look too far
backwards, but we’ve had, I think, a pretty good debate on that, actually, so far.
But retrospective or retroactive, as the case may be, we are saying that the  person
who’s deprived of their liberty is going to be subject to that designation as a “terrorist”
for longer. So how or why is that the case? Well, the answer is that if a person wants to
apply to have that designation revoked, then they can’t say, in ef fect, that they’re no
longer involved in acts that led to or would lead to designation as a terrorist. Well, if
they’re in prison, then of course they can’t—or at least they shouldn’t be able to. It would
be illogical if we were to say, “Oh well, you’re no t a terrorist any more, you know —by
the way, I hope you’re enjoying His Majesty’s accommodation —and therefore we
consider you to be a reformed person.” Of course we want a terrorist to be reformed to
the extent that they might be rehabilitated and maybe de-radicalised and encouraged and
otherwise persuaded not to engage in such evil acts. But the mere fact of them not being
able to undertake those acts while they are in prison shouldn’t count to their credit in the
determination of whether they are still a terrorist at heart.
We’re also seeing that the expiry of the designation would be paused. So a designation
as a terrorist isn’t indefinite; it’s for a certain period of time, but you don’t get to run out
the clock on that designation simply because you’re behind bars for having committed an
atrocity—for example, and actually specifically and explicitly, in the case of the March 15
terrorist.
We also see here that, as a result of this bill, it will be the case that while a person’s
imprisoned, the Prime Mini ster, no less —he or she at the time —would be required to
review every three years whether the designation is no longer justified. I know I’ve
engaged in a double negative, and I’m probably far too prone to do that, but the wording,
I think, is quite deliberate coming out of the select committee, whereby they’re using the
language of the statute to say that the test is whether or not the designation is no longer
justified. So that would be on the basis on which the designation as a terrorist would
continue to hold.
So all of that’s to do with the designation. And then you’ve got control orders. We
won’t get through all of those in the available time, but we’ve got, basically, a broader
range of objectionable publications, if we’re thinking about what would m ake a person
eligible to be subject to a control order, and also to allow a control order to cover
individuals who have been sentenced to home detention or a community-based sentence.
So if someone who commits an act that leads them to be designated as a t errorist should
have the relative good fortune of being sentenced only to home detention or a community-
based sentence, as opposed to being imprisoned in a traditional manner, then they
shouldn’t have the benefit also of avoiding a control order, if a cont rol order would be
30 Mar 2023 Counter-Terrorism Acts (Designations etc.) Amdt Bill 15801
appropriate, given what they’ve done. A control order, in sentence conditions, would be
able to apply concurrently, and I don’t have the time to state my own view on that.
But suffice to say, for the reasons that the Minister has set ou t and as my colleague
Mark Mitchell has emphasised in support, and including the fact that the Minister has
engaged diligently in a nonpartisan basis on this, we do support this bill and its continued
passage.

items.speaker: IBRAHIM OMER
items.text: I rise to take a call on the Counter -Terrorism Acts
(Designations and Control Orders) Amendment Bill. This is part of the work the
Government is doing to boost our  counter-terrorism laws to make it harder for people
who pose serious threats to New Zealanders or need to unleash terror attacks, and I’d like
to thank the Minister for bringing this bill to this House.
Now the terrorism landscape is evolving, and our law s need to reflect this reality as
well. So the designations and control orders schemes which are in line with this
Government’s commitment to implementing the recommendations of the royal
commission of inquiry into the Christchurch terror attacks in Christ church masjidain is
specifically in line with recommendation 18 which is related to counter-terrorism.
The bill also amends the regime for imposing control orders in the terrorism
suppression Act of 2019. The horrific attacks in Christchurch and LynnMall i s a
continuous reminder of the devastating consequence of terrorism on our communities and
individuals, and these are very important amendments that look to keep Aotearoa New
Zealand as safe as possible.
As young people are active more online, and terror g roups are relentlessly looking
online to radicalise the young people, we need to futureproof our legislation to make sure
that our country is being safe, and this is going to contribute to that as well. I’d like to
thank the select committee for the work t hey have done to scrutinise this bill. I’d like to
thank the submitters and the Minister for all their work to actually get this bill today in
this House, and I’d also like to thank the contributors from across the House who
positively contributed to this. So it’s a good bill; I commend it to the House.

items.speaker: BROOKE VAN VELDEN
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s a
pleasure to rise this afternoon on behalf of my ACT Party colleague Nicole McKee, who
sits on the Justice Committee and who has done a lot of good, diligent work on this bill,
but wasn’t able to be here this afternoon.
I’m rising on behalf of ACT to suppo rt the second reading of the Counter -Terrorism
Acts (Designations and Control Orders) Amendment Bill. This bill went to select
committee in October last year and was reported back in November last year, and it was
unfortunate that it was a much shorter select committee than was necessary—it was only
four weeks—but it’s great to see that even within that amount of time, over 200 people
submitted on this piece of legislation. I’m glad to see that it did get some debate, and I
know that the select committee itself was very thorough in its deliberation on this bill.
This bill is a very serious matter. It deals with terrorism in our country and how to
counter it. There are two parts to this bill, because it’s trying to seek to clarify and
strengthen our counter -terrorism legislation to better prevent and respond to terrorism
within New Zealand and any associated activities.
So the first part of this bill, which it’s hoping to change, is to change the designation
regime within the Terrorism Suppression Act to allow the Prime Minister to designate an
individual as well as a group as a terrorist entity. That is a very important change, because
currently, only groups can be considered terrorist, rather than individuals.
It’s a very important change to be made, becau se as I was reading through the debate
pack prepared by the Parliamentary Library, I noted that there have been instances since
we first put in place the counter -terrorism laws where we finally have individuals in
prison for terrorism offences, but, importantly, we have had tragedies in our own society
15802 Counter-Terrorism Acts (Designations etc.) Amdt Bill 30 Mar 2023
where individuals rather than groups have been responsible for terrorism. There are two
instances of note: those that occurred in Christchurch —the terrible, terrible events in
Christchurch—and also a man in New Lynn, and my thoughts go out to all of the families
and communities that are still suffering from the ongoing effects of these terrorist
activities.
The bill then tries to clarify what it then means to designate an individual to be part of
this law. Th at’s very important because we finally have people imprisoned, who are
individuals, and so we’ve had to define under this law what it means to be imprisoned,
and have included people aged between 14 and 17 years in the custody of the Department
of Corrections or the New Zealand Police, as well as people who might be locked up in
our normal justice system, or what people understand to be in prison.
That is very important in order to make sure that we are truly grappling with the proper
problem. It’s also very important because the Minister herself has said that “The terrorist
designation scheme was initially brought in to stop New Zealanders from providing
financial support to overseas terrorist groups in the wake of the September 11 attacks.
Now, as the terrorism landscape has evolved, our laws need to also.”
And so we do have people designated as terrorist entities imprisoned, but they still
seek to attempt to influence and incite others from behind bars overseas. That could be
our reality here in the futu re. So these laws look at what it means to designate a person,
rather than an entity, as a terrorist, and also how that will work for people behind bars.
Now, that also becomes very important because the second part of this bill seeks to
change the Terrori sm Suppression (Control Orders) Act. It allows for a larger range of
objectionable publications to be included in the eligibility test for a control order.
Now, we know that this has had some concern within the committee because there
were submitters who suggested, you know, this could mean that people who might have
an illegal online video game but don’t realise that it’s banned could in fact be in breach
of a control order. But the officials during the select committee process clarified that being
in possession of a banned game would not be enough in itself to warrant a control order
on an individual, but a whole set of other criteria also had to be made for that individual
to be considered.
So the control orders, through the select committee process, have  been extended to
cover individuals that have been sentenced to home detention or to community -based
sentences, and they’ve allowed the judges more discretion on deciding what the
requirements of those control orders should be. So it’s taking into account the fact that
every person who may have a control order placed upon them is different, and everyone
will have different unique situations and different circumstances that might need to be
controlled. So there will be also new protocols for managing electronic monitoring of an
individual subject to a control order.
Throughout the select committee process, they tidied up the bill a little way to
represent some pending enactments in other Acts that they worked on last year. T hat
included changes that were made to the Security Information in Proceedings Act, and
aligned those legislative pieces with this bill so that when they all come into force, they
will all work together. I think it’s really important that when we are chang ing our laws,
we’re making sure that they work for New Zealanders and they are comprehensive and
they work together.
The committee felt the need to clarify some electronic monitoring requirements. They
removed some of the provisions from a schedule and put it into the main body of the bill
to insert new clause 19A, which would outline where the limits on the use of electronic
monitoring would have been inserted.
Finally, when they went through the select committee process, they noted that the
Commissioner of Police was the sole and current authority for electronic monitoring. The
30 Mar 2023 Counter-Terrorism Acts (Designations etc.) Amdt Bill 15803
Department of Corrections also had a major part to play and responsibility for electronic
monitoring, so they have been referenced throughout the bill to allow them the authority,
as with the New Zealand Police.
This is a very serious bill in reference to a very serious matter. The ACT Party
commends it to the House, and we want to see New Zealand be a safe society where we
can suppress terrorism so that all New Zealanders are safe a nd our laws reflect a way of
helping people become rehabilitated while we are keeping New Zealanders safe and we
are removing threats of terrorism. Thank you, Mr Speaker.

Hon JACQUI DEAN (Assistant Speaker) : Almighty God, we give thanks for the

We have seen the horrific impact that terrorist attacks have had here in Aotearoa. Four 
years on from the terror attack on the Christchurch mosques, I want to acknowledge the 
enduring harm of terror attacks on victims in the broader Muslim community. The 
evolving threat of terrorism means that our counter-terrorism legislation must be kept up 
to date to protect our communities. The bill before us is part of the Government’s wider 
response to the recommendation made by the royal commission of inquiry into the terror 
attack on Christchurch. It enhances our counter -terrorism legislation by clarifying and 
strengthening our protections against high-risk individuals.  
I want to acknowledge the work of the Justice Committee for its diligent consideration 
of the bill. The committee received 210 submissions of whom four presented an oral 
submission. I thank those who took the time to provide a submission to the committee. 
I want to highlight the key chang es the committee made that warrant closer 
examination. The first part of the bill makes changes to the designation scheme of the 
Terrorism Suppression Act 2002 to clarify its application to imprisoned individuals. The 
second makes amendments to strengthen the control orders regime in the Terrorism 
Suppression (Control Orders) Act 2019. These amendments expand the eligibility criteria 
for a control order, give the courts more discretion when imposing conditions, and adjust 
the settings related to name suppression.  
I want to start by discussing the first part of the bill—and particularly the role that the 
Prime Minister has—with its powers to designate a group or individual that has carried 
out or participated in a terrorist act as a terrorist entity. A desig nation places restrictions 
on that group or individual, aimed at preventing them from funding or receiving funds to 
support further terrorist activities. The bill clarifies the application of the Prime Minister’s 
power in relation to renewal of a designation of an individual who is imprisoned.  
Under the current law, a prisoner must have their designation removed after three years 
if it cannot be demonstrated that they present an ongoing risk of terrorist activity. 
However, when a person is in prison, it is  the restrictions placed on them by their 
designation and incarceration that may prevent them from posing a risk. Were their 
designation to be removed, they could financially support others in carrying out terrorist 
acts. So to address this, the bill pause s the expiration of a designation whilst that person
